Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 893 exact hits in 263 files representing 259 independent works. Family check covered the elephant king's stride (象王行), backward look or turn (象王回顧／回旋), the lion's roar or vigorous motion (師子吼／奮迅), the fragrant elephant (香象), and Samantabhadra's white elephant. Stride, backward-look, mount, and narrative clauses all denote the same elephant king as animal; they change what the animal does, not what thing the headword names. The narrative white-elephant witness remains listed in SourceTexts but was not curated because it adds outside-story identity rather than defining the Chan bend.

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The elephant king appears through elephant-like gait, return, and royal-animal comparisons, distinct from the lion language paired with it.
EvidenceBody: Changlu Timing looks right and says, 'the bearing of the elephant king—how could it forget the backward look?' Other records make stride and backward look a wider public comparison: 'in the lion's den there is no other beast; where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease.' When Deshan Huiyuan mounts the seat and says 'the lion frowns; the elephant king looks back,' Kaixian Shanxian awakens, enters the room, and presents his understanding. Later verse calls the lion's vigorous motion world-shaking and the elephant king's backward look effortless. The line can also be tested rather than merely praised: when an unnamed monastic quotes 'where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease,' Yinyuan Longqi drives him out with blows. The Chan-specific bend is the deployment of a royal animal's gait and backward glance as teaching-seat bearing and encounter language. The records assign no further gloss to the image, and neither does this entry.

Senses.Explanation: The elephant king appears through elephant-like gait, return, and royal-animal comparisons, distinct from the lion language paired with it. Chan records repeatedly take the elephant king's bearing, stride, and backward look as publicly recognizable forms of Changlu Timing's conduct. Changlu Timing looks right and says, 'the bearing of the elephant king—how could it forget the backward look?' Another stock pairing says, 'in the lion's den there is no other beast; where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease.' The backward look itself enters encounter history: when Deshan Huiyuan mounts the seat and says 'the lion frowns; the elephant king looks back,' Kaixian Shanxian awakens, enters the room, and presents his understanding. Later verse calls the lion's vigorous motion world-shaking and the elephant king's backward look effortless. The line can also be tested rather than merely praised: when an unnamed monastic quotes 'where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease,' Yinyuan Longqi drives him out with blows. The Chan-specific bend is this deployment of a royal animal's gait and backward glance as teaching-seat bearing and encounter language. The records assign no further gloss to the image, and neither does this entry.
